records.sourceFile: A biopsychosocial model for understanding training load, fatigue, and musculoskeletal sport injury in university athletes - A scoping review.pdf

paper.citation: McClean ZJ, Pasanen K, Lun V, Charest J, Herzog W, Werthner P, et al. A Biopsychosocial Model for Understanding Training Load, Fatigue, and Musculoskeletal Sport Injury in University Athletes: A Scoping Review. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2024;38(6):1177-1188.
paper.abstract: The review examined training load, fatigue and musculoskeletal (MSK) injury in university athletes, then used expert consensus to build a biopsychosocial model. Ten articles were included. Key findings were an absence of injury surveillance methodology and contextual factors that can influence the training load-fatigue-MSK injury relationship. The authors highlight academic load, social load and mental health load as key variables and present an integrative model for MSK injury in university sport, with an example of causal inference applied to longitudinal observational data.
paper.tldr: Few studies of university athletes link training load, fatigue and musculoskeletal injury, and most lack consistent injury surveillance. The biopsychosocial model proposed here is a research framework that still needs to be tested.
paper.methods: A scoping review following PRISMA-ScR searched Embase, MEDLINE, PubMed and SPORTDiscus in December 2022 for English peer-reviewed studies from 2002 onward on university athletes, MSK injury, training load and fatigue. Two reviewers screened titles and abstracts independently, full texts were checked against the inclusion criteria, and reference lists added 2 articles to the 8 found by search, giving 10. Each study was appraised with the Quality Assessment Tool for Observational Cohort and Cross-Sectional Studies, and experts in sport medicine, sleep, sport psychology, biomechanics and sport science reached consensus on eight contextual factors.
paper.findings: Of 10 studies (9 NCAA, 1 U Sports; 319 participants, 14.1% female), seven examined training load and three examined fatigue. In tackle football, injury risk was higher when the acute to chronic workload ratio was 2 SD above or below the mean, and greatest at 2 SD above when perceived wellness was higher and soreness lower (Sampson et al.); in 19 basketball players, sleep duration and muscle soreness predicted injury (Watson et al.). No study examined mental health as a predictor of sport injury in university sport.
paper.limitations: The authors note inconsistent injury surveillance, no control for athlete exposure, no sex- or gender-based analysis, limited consideration of performance level, and training load used as a proxy for tissue load. Five of the 10 studies were in tackle football (four NCAA, one U Sports), two were female-only with none analysing men and women together, and two of the three fatigue studies measured throwing kinematics rather than injury. The model was not validated against data.
paper.practicalImplications: For university sport staff, the review supports recording internal and external training load together with wellness, sleep and soreness measures, and using one consistent injury surveillance method, since most studies did not. Its suggestions for baseline sleep and mental health screening and for tracking academic and social load come from the expert panel, not from the included studies, and no included study tested academic or social load as an injury predictor.
paper.athleteDev: Limited. The review maps training load and fatigue measures such as session RPE, GPS and inertial load, and wellness questionnaires, but it does not show that any load strategy improves performance. Its performance content is limited to fatigue effects on throwing kinematics and workload in extra time.
paper.rtp: Limited. The review discusses reinjury and injury etiology, but it does not evaluate return-to-sport criteria or timing. It cannot be used to decide when an athlete is fit to return from injury.

records.sourceFile: Activity distribution among the hamstring muscles during high‐speed running - A descriptive multichannel surface EMG study.pdf

paper.citation: Suskens JJM, Tol JL, Kerkhoffs GMMJ, Maas H, van Dieën JH, Reurink G. Activity distribution among the hamstring muscles during high-speed running: a descriptive multichannel surface EMG study. 2023.
paper.abstract: Purpose: to assess activity distribution among the hamstring muscles during high-speed running, comparing within and between muscle activity, relative contribution, and hip and knee angles at peak activity. Methods: multichannel EMG of male basketball players on a treadmill at 15 locations (five biceps femoris long head, four semitendinosus, six semimembranosus). Results: 29 non-injured players (mean age 17 years). Heterogeneous activity was found within every hamstring muscle; in late swing, semimembranosus activity and relative contribution were higher than semitendinosus. Hip and knee angles at peak activity did not differ. Conclusion: hamstrings were most active in late swing, with the semimembranosus most active and the semitendinosus least active; the most proximal biceps femoris long head region was more active in late swing, and peak activity occurred at similar joint angles.
paper.tldr: In uninjured male basketball players sprinting on a treadmill, hamstring activity was uneven within each muscle, peaked in late swing, and was lowest in the semitendinosus. Use this as a description of normal activation, not a measure of injury risk.
paper.methods: A sub-study of an RCT (NL7248) in male basketball players aged 16 or older without hamstring injury in the prior 12 months, drawn from the trial's control and Nordic hamstring exercise arms. Fifteen surface EMG electrode pairs (five biceps femoris long head, four semitendinosus, six semimembranosus) were placed on the left leg and normalized to the peak of three MVIC trials in one prone knee-flexion position. Motion capture (100 Hz) defined early-swing, late-swing and stance phases in three strides at the highest maintained treadmill speed, and activity was tested with one-dimensional statistical parametric mapping and repeated-measures ANOVA, and joint angles at peak activity with repeated-measures ANOVA.
paper.findings: Of 38 eligible trial participants, one did not attend and eight had unusable marker data, leaving 29 for analysis; within biceps femoris long head, the most proximal electrode had higher activity than all other locations (F(4,112) = 4.68). Semitendinosus activity was lower than both other muscles in early swing and lower than semimembranosus in late swing (F(2,56) = 7.31), and its relative contribution was lower than both in early and late swing (F(2,56) = 7.28). All peak activity occurred in late swing at mean hip 65.4 degrees and knee 57.3 degrees, with no significant differences in joint angle between muscles or locations.
paper.limitations: Only uninjured players were tested, two had prior ACL injuries (one with semitendinosus graft), and participants from the parent trial's control and Nordic hamstring exercise arms were pooled without analysis by arm. Surface EMG cross-talk cannot be fully excluded, a single MVIC position was used for normalization, the harness added about 4 kg, running was on a treadmill, and the late-swing between-muscle difference disappeared with SENIAM electrode placement. The PDF is an accepted manuscript that prints no journal name or issue year, so 2023 comes from the Crossref record and the download stamp.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff screening or rehabilitating hamstrings may note that late swing is the phase of highest activity in uninjured players at near-maximal running speed, and that the proximal region of the biceps femoris long head is its most active region there. The study does not test whether injury-prevention or rehabilitation exercises change this distribution, so it should not be used to select exercises on its own.
paper.athleteDev: Limited. The study describes muscle activation in uninjured players at near-maximal running speed, but it does not test whether training changes activation or improves sprint performance. It supports understanding how the hamstrings share activity during sprinting, not prescribing a load.
paper.rtp: Limited. Because only uninjured players were studied, the paper cannot set return-to-running or hamstring readiness criteria, and it does not show that activation patterns after injury return to normal. It may inform future studies that compare activation in injured and uninjured athletes.

records.sourceFile: Incidence of acute hamstring injuries in soccer - A systematic review of 13 studies involving more than 3800 athletes with 2 million sport exposure hours.pdf

paper.citation: Diemer WM, Winters M, Tol JL, Pas HIMFL, Moen MH. Incidence of acute hamstring injuries in soccer: a systematic review of 13 studies involving more than 3800 athletes with 2 million sport exposure hours. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2021.
paper.abstract: Thirteen prospective studies of adult soccer players were summarized descriptively to estimate acute hamstring injury incidence and recurrence. Incidence was 0.3 to 1.9 per 1000 exposure hours, and recurrence ranged from 4% to 68%, with certainty of evidence rated from moderate to very low.
paper.tldr: Acute hamstring injuries in soccer occur at roughly 0.3 to 1.9 per 1000 exposure hours in training and matches. The wide range reflects inconsistent injury definitions and exposure recording, so compare your own data with these figures only after matching definitions.
paper.methods: PRISMA-guided systematic review, prospectively registered in PROSPERO. Five databases were searched to August 2019 without language or date limits, and two reviewers screened and extracted data. Eligible studies were prospective, in adult soccer players, and reported acute hamstring injuries with exposure hours. Quality was assessed with a modified Newcastle-Ottawa scale and certainty with GRADE.
paper.findings: Incidence was 0.4 to 1.9 per 1000 hours with time-loss definitions and 0.3 to 1.0 with tissue-based definitions. Professional players had 0.5 to 1.9 per 1000 hours with time-loss definitions, and women in two studies had 0.3 to 0.5. Acute hamstring injuries made up 5% to 15% of all soccer injuries across seven studies, and recurrence ranged from 4% to 68% depending on the definition and follow-up window. Certainty was very low for most measures, low for women and moderate only for the single-study professional tissue-definition estimate.
paper.limitations: The authors note the small number of studies, heterogeneous methods, exclusion of studies without exposure hours, and very low certainty for most measures. The abstract and results give 5% to 15% of injuries while the Conclusions and Key Points give 5% to 13%, and the record uses the results value.
paper.practicalImplications: Use the 0.3 to 1.9 per 1000 hour range as a rough benchmark for how common acute hamstring injuries are in soccer. Record exposure in minutes, code injuries to the muscle group, and state whether a time-loss or tissue definition is used, so that your own surveillance can be compared with published rates.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: the review gives no training intervention. Its use for performance staff is to set up injury surveillance with exposure hours, muscle-specific injury definitions and, where possible, intensity measures, so that squad data can be compared later.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: the review does not set return-to-play timelines. It reports recurrence of 4% to 68% and notes that recurrence definitions drive those rates, so the figures should be interpreted cautiously and not used alone for return decisions.

records.sourceFile: Initial assessment and management of select musculoskeletal injuries - A Team Physician Consensus Statement - 2024.pdf

paper.citation: Herring SA, Kibler WB, Putukian M, Boyajian-O'Neill LA, Chang CJ, Franks RR, et al. Initial Assessment and Management of Select Musculoskeletal Injuries: A Team Physician Consensus Statement. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2024;23(3):86-104.
paper.abstract: The Team Physician Consensus Conference summarizes initial assessment and management of select musculoskeletal injuries in athletes. Each topic covers mechanism, clinical presentation, evaluation, nonoperative and operative options and injury risk modification, with statements labelled essential or desirable.
paper.tldr: This is a practical reference for the first assessment and early management of shoulder dislocation, UCL, hamstring, ACL, meniscus, ankle, groin and apophyseal injuries. It is a consensus guide rather than a graded evidence review, so check specific decisions against current literature.
paper.methods: Expert consensus. An executive committee selected topics and drafted an outline, representatives of six professional organizations reviewed the literature for each topic, and statements were agreed by unanimous consensus at in-person meetings before board approval. The statement was co-published in Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise (2024;56(3):385-401). No systematic review, levels of evidence or recommendation grades were included.
paper.findings: Each topic lists essential information every team physician should know and desirable information for ideal settings. Nonoperative care is the initial approach for most disabled throwing shoulder and UCL presentations, with UCL surgery reserved for high-demand overhead athletes or failed nonoperative care, and most hamstring injuries are treated nonoperatively, with surgery for specific proximal tendon tears and displaced avulsions. The statement reports that multimodal prevention programs reduce ACL and hamstring injury, that eccentric strength training reduces hamstring injury risk, and that core stabilizing exercise reduces load and injury risk.
paper.limitations: The authors state that the statement is not a standard of care and is general in nature, that only select topics are included, and that no systematic review or evidence grading was done. Several sections note limited high-quality evidence, including for biologic and corticosteroid injections, stretching as a risk modifier, and biologic therapy for UCL injury.
paper.practicalImplications: Use the essential points as a first-assessment checklist: confirm the mechanism, examine neurovascular status, obtain the imaging named for each injury, and set referral criteria. Treat the surgical indications as triggers for referral rather than default plans.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: the workload and kinetic-chain sections, which cover monitoring load and screening the whole kinetic chain for throwing shoulder and UCL injury, can guide load planning for throwers. For hamstring risk, the statement lists eccentric strength training, core stabilizing exercise, multimodal programs such as FIFA 11, and monitoring load and fatigue.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: the statement gives few return timelines. It says same-day return may be considered for some athletes with recurrent shoulder dislocation (easy relocation, little pain, full motion and protective strength), that most athletes are out of overhead sport for 12 months or longer after UCL reconstruction, that throwers need a specific throwing protocol, and that return to high-risk sport after ACL surgery should wait until the athlete is physically and psychologically ready.

records.sourceFile: Load, Overload, and Recovery in the Athlete- Select Issues for the Team PhysicianVA Consensus Statement.pdf

paper.citation: Herring SA, Kibler WB, Putukian M, et al. Load, Overload, and Recovery in the Athlete: Select Issues for the Team Physician: A Consensus Statement. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2019;18(4):141-148.
paper.abstract: This consensus statement, developed by six professional sports medicine associations, reviews load, overload and recovery in athletes. It covers current concepts, medical, musculoskeletal and psychosocial issues, measurement and monitoring, and intervention strategies, including recovery modalities. It states that it is a general guide and not a standard of care.
paper.tldr: A six-association team physician consensus on how training and competition load can lead to overload injury and illness, and how to manage that load. It is a general guide, and several monitoring tools and recovery modalities have limited evidence.
paper.methods: Consensus statement written by an executive committee and expert panel for six sports medicine associations. The text does not describe a systematic literature search or a formal grading process.
paper.findings: Load is described as external work and internal individual response, and overload occurs when the two become unbalanced. Abrupt or excessive load and competitive calendar congestion are linked to bone stress injury, tendinopathy, physeal injury, respiratory illness and sleep disruption. Overtraining is described with physical and psychosocial symptoms; the text states that a single hormonal measure cannot diagnose it and that HRV findings are mixed, with interpretation still evolving.
paper.limitations: No original data, sample or effect sizes are reported, and the document says it is not a standard of care. The text states that many monitoring technologies need more research on accuracy and on whether they improve performance or reduce injury.
paper.practicalImplications: Team physicians should monitor both external load and the athlete's internal response, using subjective measures such as RPE and mood alongside objective ones. When internal overload factors are unfavorable, they should work with the athletic care network to adjust training and competition load. Load management tools named in the text include periodization, limits on weekly training and game frequency, pitch or serve counts, and sleep and nutrition support.
paper.athleteDev: Use the load concepts (external load, internal load, and overload) to plan training progression, and watch for overtraining signs such as a performance plateau, disturbed sleep, elevated resting heart rate and slow recovery. The statement says subjective measures such as RPE and mood have shown superior sensitivity and consistency over some objective measures for detecting changes in wellbeing.
paper.rtp: The statement covers musculoskeletal overload, including bone stress injuries and tendinopathy, and the need to adjust load when internal overload factors are unfavorable. It gives no return-to-sport criteria, testing thresholds or timelines, so it cannot be used to decide when an injured athlete is ready to return.

records.sourceFile: Pain Medication Data from the 2021 and 2022 National Football League Prescription Drug Monitoring Program.pdf

paper.citation: Hill KP, Kroenke K, Wasserman EB, et al. Pain Medication Data from the 2021 and 2022 National Football League Prescription Drug Monitoring Program. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2024;23(10):348-351.
paper.abstract: This report presents 2021 and 2022 prescription drug monitoring program data on pain medications, including over-the-counter drugs, issued to NFL players by club physicians or external providers. Of 3,142 players under contract in 2021, 2,207 received 14,903 pain medication prescriptions, and in 2022, 2,189 of 3,152 players received 14,880. Most prescriptions were for NSAIDs (85.1%), and only 2.9% were for opioids.
paper.tldr: In the 2021 and 2022 NFL seasons, about 70% of players received at least one pain medication prescription. NSAIDs made up about 85% of prescriptions and opioids about 3%, with about 10% of players receiving an opioid each season. These are prescriptions entered in the league record, not confirmed use.
paper.methods: Descriptive analysis of pain medication prescriptions recorded in the NFL prescription drug monitoring program, an electronic medical record, for players under contract from training camp through the end of each season. Prescriptions were grouped into eight drug classes from NDC-to-GPI mapping, and counts, percentages and unique players were calculated in SAS. Dose, strength and pill count were not used in the prevalence counts.
paper.findings: In 2021, 14,903 prescriptions were issued to 2,207 of 3,142 players (70.2%), and in 2022, 14,880 to 2,189 of 3,152 (69.4%). NSAIDs accounted for 84.6% and 85.5% of prescriptions in the two seasons, and opioids for 3.1% and 2.7%. Opioids were prescribed to 319 players (10.2%) in 2021 and 300 (9.5%) in 2022, and 576 different players received an opioid across the two seasons. The mean number of tablets per opioid prescription was 17.7 in 2021 and 18.4 in 2022. The authors judge opioid prevalence (about 10% of players per season) to be similar to U.S. population data from the early 2010s and lower than the 14.8% annual rate reported for men aged 25 to 34, but these comparisons use different time frames and data sources.
paper.limitations: The data are not claims data, so filled or taken medication is unknown, and dose, strength and indication are not captured. The authors note that outside prescriptions may be under-reported and that only OTC medications provided by club physicians are recorded. They state that no comparable professional contact-sport PDMP data exist, which makes it hard to place the results in a more specific context.
paper.practicalImplications: Medical staff can track prescription counts by drug class across seasons for monitoring and education, which is the purpose the authors give for the program. Because the data show prescriptions rather than use, they should not be used to judge individual players or the safety of prescribing without outcome data.
paper.athleteDev: The data do not measure performance, so they do not inform training or performance decisions. Staff who manage player medication may use the drug-class breakdown as a benchmark for prescribing patterns, while recognizing that it reflects prescriptions, not performance effects.
paper.rtp: The data cover all prescriptions for players under contract, with no injury type, time-loss or clearance information, so they cannot be used to judge return to sport. They describe prescribing patterns only and set no return-to-play criteria.

records.sourceFile: Progressive Workload Periodization Maximizes Effects of Nordic Hamstring Exercise on Muscle Injury Risk Factors.pdf

paper.citation: Severo-Silveira L, Dornelles MP, Lima-e-Silva FX, Marchiori CL, Medeiros TM, Pappas E, et al. Progressive Workload Periodization Maximizes Effects of Nordic Hamstring Exercise on Muscle Injury Risk Factors. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2018.
paper.abstract: The study compared constant and progressive workload 8-week Nordic hamstring exercise programs in 21 rugby union players on hamstring strength and biceps femoris long head architecture. Only the progressive group increased hamstring strength and hamstring-to-quadriceps ratios, while both groups increased muscle thickness and fascicle length. The authors conclude that progressive workload was superior for strength and fascicle length, although the between-group differences were not statistically significant.
paper.tldr: Nordic hamstring training improved hamstring muscle size and length in these rugby players whether the workload was constant or progressive. Only the progressive program also improved hamstring strength and hamstring-to-quadriceps ratios, but the between-group differences were not statistically significant.
paper.methods: Thirty-seven eligible players from one rugby union squad agreed to participate, and 21 completed a randomly allocated constant or progressive workload 8-week Nordic hamstring program (two sessions per week, no untrained control) and were analysed. Isokinetic knee strength and biceps femoris long head thickness, pennation angle and fascicle length (ultrasound) were measured before and after, with both legs pooled. Within-group change used paired t-tests and Cohen's d, and between-group percent changes used independent t-tests and magnitude-based inference.
paper.findings: Only the progressive group increased concentric hamstring peak torque (7.7%, p = 0.004, d = 0.42) and eccentric hamstring peak torque (6.9%, p = 0.041, d = 0.39), along with conventional (7.6%, p = 0.015) and functional (6.6%, p = 0.026) hamstring-to-quadriceps ratios. Both groups increased biceps femoris long head thickness (about 7%) and fascicle length, with the constant group rising from 10.48 to 11.26 cm and the progressive group from 11.13 to 12.26 cm. No between-group difference was statistically significant.
paper.limitations: Of 37 enrolled players, 16 were lost (10 injured, 2 ill, 4 transferred) and only completers were analysed. Group sizes are reported inconsistently (text 11 constant and 10 progressive, Table 1 10 and 11, matching 20 and 22 legs), legs rather than players were the unit of analysis, and the abstract gives an 8% constant-group fascicle length gain where Table 1 gives 7.44%. There is no untrained control, no injury outcome and no significant between-group difference; the PDF prints 2018 while Crossref lists 2021.
paper.practicalImplications: Both Nordic hamstring programs were followed by increases in biceps femoris long head fascicle length and thickness in these rugby players, and only the progressive program was followed by gains in hamstring strength and hamstring-to-quadriceps ratios. Because the progressive advantage was not statistically significant and there was no untrained control, staff should treat progression as a sensible way to plan the program rather than a proven way to prevent injury.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: A progressed Nordic hamstring block is a reasonable default, since only the progressive group showed significant within-group strength gains and the strength advantage was rated likely by magnitude-based inference, though not statistically significant. The paper shows the progression scheme only in a figure, so take the exact sets and repetitions from the source.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It tested risk factors in players without current injuries and reports no rehabilitation, reinjury or return-to-play outcomes, so it cannot show when an injured hamstring is ready for competition.

records.sourceFile: Proximal rectus femoris tendon tear in a professional football placekicker - A case report.pdf

paper.citation: Noble-Taylor K, Price M, McInnis K. Proximal Rectus Femoris Tendon Tear in a Professional Football Placekicker: A Case Report. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2023;22(6):187-190.
paper.abstract: The authors describe a proximal rectus femoris tendon tear in a professional American football placekicker, with imaging, surgical repair and return to kicking. The tear involved both the direct and indirect heads, which is rarely reported in this sport. The athlete returned to running and pain-free kicking at about 6 months.
paper.tldr: A professional placekicker with a near-complete proximal rectus femoris tear returned to pain-free kicking about 6 months after surgical repair. This single case shows one successful surgical route, but it does not settle the choice between surgery and nonoperative care.
paper.methods: A case report of one professional placekicker, with clinical examination, point-of-care ultrasound and MRI at presentation. The athlete then underwent open surgical repair 2 weeks after injury at an outside clinic, followed by a graduated rehabilitation program with follow-up at 6 months.
paper.findings: Ultrasound showed near-complete disruption of the direct head with about 1 cm of retraction, and MRI showed a high-grade near full-thickness partial tear of the direct and indirect attachments. The athlete was non-weight-bearing for 6 weeks after surgery, began eccentric strengthening at 8 weeks, returned to kicking at 3 months and had a minor hip flexion deficit at 6 months.
paper.limitations: Only one athlete is described, with a single 6-month follow-up, no measured strength values and no report of return to competitive play. The authors cite two NFL punter cases, an 11-athlete NFL case series with no pure placekickers, and professional soccer surgical reports, so the evidence base for placekickers is thin.
paper.practicalImplications: For a kicker with a near-complete proximal rectus femoris tear, this case shows a surgical route with progressive hip motion, isometric then eccentric loading, and a return to kicking at about 3 months. The authors stress that the choice between surgery and nonoperative care depends on injury timing, career stage and goals, so staff should use this as one example of the process rather than a timeline to follow.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: This case gives one kicker's sequence after surgical repair: non-weight-bearing for 6 weeks, eccentric strengthening from about week 8 and kicking from month 3. It is useful for planning kicking work after a similar injury, but it is one athlete's timeline, not a standard for placekickers.
paper.rtp: The case gives one surgical return-to-kicking timeline: kicking from 3 months and pain-free running and kicking at 6 months with a minor hip flexion deficit. The paper does not report return to competitive play or the criteria used to clear this athlete, and it cannot set a timeline for other kickers or for nonoperative care.

records.sourceFile: Scheduling of eccentric lower limb injury prevention exercises during the soccer micro-cycle - Which day of the week.pdf

paper.citation: Lovell R, Whalan M, Marshall PWM, Sampson JA, Siegler JC, Buchheit M. Scheduling of Eccentric Lower-limb Injury Prevention Exercises during the Soccer micro-cycle: Which day of the week? 2018.
paper.abstract: Eighteen semi-professional players were monitored over three 6-day micro-cycles, with an eccentric lower-limb injury prevention program given 1 or 3 days after a match and compared with a control cycle. Creatine kinase, hamstring and quadriceps soreness, isometric strength and jump performance were tracked for five days after each match.
paper.tldr: Doing the eccentric injury prevention program one day after a match slowed the drop in creatine kinase without raising soreness beyond normal recovery. Doing it three days after a match raised creatine kinase and hamstring soreness on the days before the next match.
paper.methods: Randomized, counterbalanced crossover study: each player completed a control micro-cycle and two micro-cycles with the program at MD+1 or MD+3 across three in-season weeks. Daily measures were capillary creatine kinase, visual-analogue hamstring and quadriceps soreness, isometric posterior-chain peak force and counter-movement jump, with session-RPE for all sessions and GPS external load recorded during matches. Outcomes were analysed with linear mixed models adjusted for baseline and sRPE, and reported as magnitude-based inferences.
paper.findings: CK was about 256% of baseline 24 h after the match in all trials. Scheduling at MD+1 slowed the CK decline at MD+2 (197% vs 142% control and 166% at MD+3). Scheduling at MD+3 raised CK on MD+4 (260% vs 146% control and 151% MD+1) and MD+5 (209% vs 125% and 127%), and hamstring soreness was higher on MD+4 (26.9 vs 7.0 control and 8.2 MD+1 AU) and MD+5 (22.5 vs 9.5 and 7.1 AU), with effects described as small to moderate. Peak force and jump measures showed no between-trial differences, and CMJ height was 3.7% lower than baseline 24 h after the match in all trials.
paper.limitations: The program was standardized and not tailored to individual training history, and match loads could not be controlled; match total distance and high-speed running were likely lower in the MD+3 trial (Table 2), and some players were substitutes or early withdrawals. CK is a nonspecific damage marker, and the neuromuscular tests were not very sensitive to match play. The PDF is the accepted manuscript and prints no year, journal name or pages, so the 2018 year comes from the Crossref record and the citation omits journal and pages.
paper.practicalImplications: For weekly fixtures, the data favour an eccentric lower-limb program on the day after a match over one three days after, because the later timing left CK and hamstring soreness higher the day before the next match. The study measured no injury outcome for either timing, so the findings support a scheduling choice, not a claim that the program prevents injury.
paper.athleteDev: In semi-professional soccer, the data suggest placing eccentric lower-limb work the day after a match rather than three days after, since the later timing raised creatine kinase and soreness before the next match. Strength and jump measures were not affected by either timing.
paper.rtp: The study cannot inform return to sport. It used semi-professional players in a training study and did not test injured athletes or return-to-play criteria; one player withdrew after a contact injury during a match, and no rehabilitation data are reported.

records.sourceFile: Shoulder Instability in Contact and Collision Athletes - A Focused Review on Assessment, Management, and Treatment.pdf

paper.citation: Sylvester JE, Reynolds CA, Wallace KG, Garzone AJ, Kamath GV. Shoulder Instability in Contact and Collision Athletes: A Focused Review on Assessment, Management, and Treatment. Curr Sports Med Rep. 2025;24(9):298-304.
paper.abstract: Glenohumeral instability is common in contact and collision athletes, and male sex, younger age at first dislocation and contact sport participation are risk factors for recurrence. The review concludes that management is individualized and based on shared decision-making, with nonoperative care allowing same-season return but carrying high recurrence risk.
paper.tldr: Shoulder instability in contact athletes is best managed with shared decision-making that weighs age, position, level, timing and recurrence risk. Nonoperative care can keep an athlete in the season but recurrence is common, and bone loss pattern (on-track or off-track lesions) helps decide on surgery.
paper.methods: Focused narrative review of shoulder instability in contact and collision athletes. The paper covers biomechanics, risk factors, sideline reduction and immobilization, imaging (radiographs, MRI, MRA and 3D CT), in-season nonoperative management, operative options (arthroscopic repair, Latarjet, remplissage and bone grafting), the GTIMS prognostic score, and bracing. No search method is described.
paper.findings: The authors report that male sex, younger age at first dislocation and contact sport participation predict recurrence, and that each year of younger age at first instability raises recurrence risk by 4.1% in one cited study. Nonoperative care returned 70% of NCAA athletes to play within 5 days, but recurrent instability was seen in 64%; a cited meta-analysis of patients aged 15-25 found redislocation rates of 16.1% after operative and 24.8% after nonoperative care. Bracing can provide up to an 80% return-to-play rate but does not significantly reduce recurrence. A GTIMS score of 4 or more suggests augmentation may be superior to Bankart repair.
paper.limitations: The review states no search strategy, so completeness cannot be judged. Several cited outcome figures come from high school or NCAA cohorts, single studies, or surveys of surgeon opinion, and the authors say their nonoperative recommendation is a judgement from their group. The text gives no numeric return-to-play criteria.
paper.practicalImplications: After a first dislocation in a contact athlete, the review supports a shared decision between athlete, family, coaches and medical team that weighs age, position, level, timing in the season and recurrence risk. Obtain 3D CT when bone loss is suspected, because glenoid track classification and a GTIMS score of 4 or more can point toward augmentation rather than Bankart repair.
paper.athleteDev: The review has little direct performance content. Its relevant point for performance staff is that bracing may allow a player to finish a season but can impede performance in overhead athletes.
paper.rtp: The review's return-to-play guidance is that athletes should show full range of motion, strength and no apprehension on provocative tests before returning. It reports that operative stabilization gives higher return-to-play success in contact athletes and that nonoperative care can allow same-season return with high recurrence, so the choice should be weighed against recurrence risk and the season timing, not return alone.

records.sourceFile: Sports-related Concussion V Genetic Factors copy.pdf

paper.citation: McGrew CA. Sports-related Concussion - Genetic Factors. Curr Sports Med Rep. 2019;18(1):20-22.
paper.abstract: Genetic biomarkers have been studied for predicting risk of sports-related concussion and for prognosis of recovery. Results from mostly small pilot studies are mixed and not yet replicated, so genetic testing should be considered investigational rather than routine.
paper.tldr: Genetic markers such as APOE, IL-6R and GRIN2A have been linked to concussion risk or slower recovery in small studies, but results are mixed and unreplicated. Genetic testing for concussion should be considered investigational and not used in clinical management.
paper.methods: Narrative review of genetic association studies of sports-related concussion and traumatic brain injury, covering susceptibility, recovery and long-term sequelae, ethical and legal concerns about testing, and athletes' interest in testing. No search method is described.
paper.findings: The largest prospective cohort cited (1,056 college athletes) linked IL-6R CC genotype with about three times the concussion risk and APOE4 with about 40% lower risk. Smaller studies of college athletes linked APOE4 with symptom scores, GRIN2A variants with recovery over 60 days (87 athletes) and an SLC17A7 variant with prolonged recovery (40 athletes), while other genotype findings were not associated with risk. The author concludes that the genetic association literature is inconsistent and needs large, well-designed prospective studies such as genome-wide association studies.
paper.limitations: The review does not describe its literature search or study selection, and it is brief, so the evidence base is only partly covered. The author notes that most cited studies have small samples and high or moderate risk of bias, and several associations come from TBI or military samples rather than sports concussion.
paper.practicalImplications: Genetic testing should not be used in routine concussion care to predict risk or recovery, because the author states it cannot yet be endorsed as a clinical tool. If athletes ask about genetic tests, staff can explain that the evidence is preliminary; the author notes that athletes often misunderstand testing protocols, counseling and legal issues, and that GINA 2008 limits use of genetic information by health insurers and employers.
paper.athleteDev: The review does not provide a performance application. The author warns that genetic information could be used to deny athletes participation or equal chances for playing time, scholarships or contracts, so it should not inform selection or training decisions.
paper.rtp: The review gives no return-to-play guidance. It reports that some genotypes, such as GRIN2A and SLC17A7 variants, have been linked to longer recovery in small studies, but these findings are preliminary and cannot guide return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Sprinting technique and hamstring strain injuries - A concept mapping study.pdf

paper.citation: Kalema RN, Duhig SJ, Williams MD, Donaldson A, Shield AJ. Sprinting technique and hamstring strain injuries: A concept mapping study. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2021.
paper.abstract: Experts in sprint coaching, physiotherapy, strength and conditioning and research used concept mapping to identify the sprinting technique components they believe raise hamstring strain injury (HSI) risk. Five clusters emerged, and training prescription was rated most important and the most confidently addressable, led by the statement 'low exposure to maximal sprint running'.
paper.tldr: In this expert panel, training prescription, especially low exposure to maximal sprinting, ranked above technique as the main HSI risk component. Treat this as expert opinion to discuss and test with your own athletes, not as proof of cause.
paper.methods: Twenty-three experts brainstormed statements online, and the research team refined them to 60. Nineteen participants sorted the statements into groups (two sorters were later excluded for not following instructions), and 20 and 19 participants rated each statement for importance and confidence. Multidimensional scaling and hierarchical cluster analysis produced an eight-cluster map that the research team reduced to five clusters.
paper.findings: The clusters, in order of mean importance, were training prescription (3.79), neuromuscular and tendon properties (3.09), kinematics and technical skills (2.99), kinetics (2.85) and hip mechanics (2.70). The statement 'low exposure to max running speed' had the highest importance rating (4.55) and shared the highest confidence rating (4.42) with 'inappropriate training programming'. Sprint coaches rated the kinematics cluster higher for importance, and academics rated the kinetics cluster higher.
paper.limitations: Experts were recruited non-randomly from professional networks, the sample was small, and the research team's judgement shaped statement synthesis and cluster boundaries, as the authors acknowledge. Participant numbers differ by step (19 sorted, 20 rated importance, 19 rated confidence, 18 completed all four steps), and two sorters were excluded. Crossref lists 2022, but the PDF is a pre-issue version that prints only 2021 on the copyright line, so 2021 is kept. The design cannot test whether these components predict injury.
paper.practicalImplications: The panel points coaches and clinicians first to training prescription, especially maximal-speed exposure and how high-speed running load is managed, when planning hamstring prevention and rehabilitation. Eccentric control of the hamstrings in the swing phase and technique items such as anterior pelvic tilt ranked lower, and the authors note the evidence on anterior pelvic tilt is mixed. Use these items as hypotheses to monitor in your own athletes.
paper.athleteDev: For performance staff, the panel favours enough maximal-speed running and deliberate management of high-speed running load as the first hamstring prevention lever, with technique such as swing-phase control and pelvic position as a second focus. These are expert opinions, so track how athletes respond rather than applying them as fixed rules.
paper.rtp: This study cannot guide return-to-sport decisions. It reports what experts believe about prevention and does not test rehabilitation or return-to-sprinting criteria in injured athletes, so it should not be used to set sprint milestones after injury.

records.sourceFile: The effect of fresh and used ankle taping on lower limb biomechanics in sports specfic movements.pdf

paper.citation: Utku B, Bähr G, Knoke H, et al. The effect of fresh and used ankle taping on lower limb biomechanics in sports specific movements. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2024.
paper.abstract: This randomized repeated-measures study examined how ankle taping, applied fresh and after 15 minutes of sports-specific use, affects lower limb biomechanics in 25 healthy participants. Fresh and used tape significantly reduced peak ankle inversion, and fresh tape increased the peak loading rate of the ground reaction force. The authors conclude that taping protects the ankle by reducing sprain-related risk factors without substantially increasing most ACL or running overuse risk factors.
paper.tldr: Ankle tape reduced peak ankle inversion in drop jumps and change-of-direction movements, and the effect was still present after 15 minutes of use. The tape also increased the loading rate of ground reaction force in all three movements, which may raise overuse risk, although the practical significance of this is unclear.
paper.methods: Twenty-five healthy participants (10 women, 15 men) completed drop jumps (25 cm), running (4.5 m/s), and 180 degree change-of-direction tasks barefoot under three conditions: no tape, fresh standard ankle taping, and taping after 15 minutes of sports-specific activity. Barefoot and fresh-tape conditions were randomized in order, and the used-tape condition always came last. Three-dimensional kinematics and force-plate kinetics were analysed with repeated-measures ANOVAs with sex as a between-subject factor and Bonferroni-corrected post-hoc t-tests.
paper.findings: Fresh tape significantly reduced peak ankle inversion in change of direction (15.4 degrees barefoot vs 11.3 degrees fresh) and drop jump (12.3 vs 9.1 degrees), and used tape still reduced it (12.6 and 10.4 degrees). Fresh tape significantly increased the peak loading rate of the resultant ground reaction force in change of direction (544.5 vs 643.5 N/kg/s), drop jump (516.9 vs 589.1 N/kg/s) and running (726.8 vs 758.8 N/kg/s), and the increase was still present with used tape in change of direction and running. In running, tape also reduced peak ankle eversion and eversion range of motion; most knee and hip variables, including peak knee adduction moment, did not change significantly.
paper.limitations: The sample was healthy volunteers without chronic ankle instability, and all movements were performed barefoot, so the results may not transfer to shod play. Only three movements, one taping technique and one 15-minute use period were studied, and tape material integrity after use was not analysed. The study measured biomechanical risk factors rather than injury outcomes. The used-tape condition always came last, so fatigue may have affected it, and some text and table statistics disagree (for example, the text reports a tape-by-sex interaction for running loading rate, while Table 3 gives an interaction p of 0.096).
paper.practicalImplications: Freshly applied tape reduces peak ankle inversion in sports-specific movements, and that restriction is still partly present after 15 minutes of use. Staff who tape ankles should also note that the loading-rate increase seen with tape is a possible overuse concern, so the trade-off should be considered for athletes who run a lot.
paper.athleteDev: Use this study to understand how tape changes ankle motion during jumping, cutting and running. Loading rate stayed higher than barefoot after 15 minutes of use in cutting and running, but longer sessions and shod movement were not tested.
paper.rtp: The study tested healthy volunteers, not injured athletes or those with chronic ankle instability, so it cannot establish whether taping is appropriate for an athlete returning to sport after an ankle injury.

records.sourceFile: The effects of on-field heat index and altitude on concussion assessments and recovery among NCAA athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Lempke LB, Lynall RC, Le RK, McCrea M, McAllister T, Schmidt JD; CARE Consortium Investigators. The Effects of On-Field Heat Index and Altitude on Concussion Assessments and Recovery Among NCAA Athletes. Sports Medicine. 2020.
paper.abstract: In 187 NCAA athletes concussed during competition, on-field altitude did not predict any acute assessment or recovery outcome. Higher heat index at the time of injury was associated with slightly shorter symptom and clinical recovery, and the authors describe these effects as small and probably not clinically meaningful.
paper.tldr: Altitude at the time of concussion (below 2,500 m) did not affect acute tests or recovery in collegiate athletes. Hotter conditions at injury were linked to a small reduction in recovery time, which the authors judge unlikely to be clinically meaningful.
paper.methods: Retrospective cohort from the CARE Consortium (2014 to 2018) of athletes with a first concussion during outdoor, in-season competition who had baseline and post-injury assessments. Air temperature and humidity were taken from Weather Underground and converted to heat index, and altitude came from Google Earth Pro. Multiple linear regressions, adjusted for age, sex and concussion history, tested heat index and altitude against SCAT, BESS and ImPACT changes within 48 hours and against days to symptom and clinical recovery.
paper.findings: Altitude (median 181 m, range -0.6 to 2,202 m) did not predict any outcome (p of 0.265 or higher). Heat index (median 17.8 C) was associated with fewer days to symptom recovery (estimate -0.1, p = 0.047, R2 = 0.06) and clinical recovery (estimate -0.3, p = 0.010, model R2 = 0.09), and male sex was associated with shorter clinical recovery (-3.7 days, p = 0.040); concussion history was not significant in these models. The acute SCAT, BESS and ImPACT models were not significant (model p of 0.200 or higher), although heat index was a significant term for ImPACT reaction time (p = 0.039) within a non-significant model. In post-hoc models, heat index was not significant for home games, and for away games it was significant only for clinical recovery (p = 0.006).
paper.limitations: Core temperature was not measured, so heat index was used as a proxy, and the authors did not control for acclimatization, travel or season timing. The heat index effect is reported inconsistently: the abstract and text give 0.05 and 0.14 days per degree with p = 0.047 and 0.006, while Table 3 gives -0.1 and -0.3 days with p = 0.047 and 0.010 (0.006 is the model p); this summary uses Table 3. Samples for some acute measures fell below 100, most injuries occurred below 500 m, and no injuries occurred at true high altitude. The PDF year is 2020, while Crossref lists 2021 for the separate correction notice.
paper.practicalImplications: Within the altitudes studied (all below 2,500 m and mostly below 500 m), altitude at the time of concussion was not linked to acute test results or recovery time. Hotter conditions at injury were linked to slightly faster recovery, not worse outcomes, but the authors judge this not clinically meaningful, so it should not change return-to-play decisions. Heat index was used as a proxy, so this does not show how core temperature affects concussion recovery.
paper.athleteDev: The findings give performance staff no basis to change post-concussion training around altitude or heat, since the study did not measure training load, acclimatization or core temperature. Its data cover only concussion recovery timelines.
paper.rtp: Altitude at injury had no association with days to symptom or clinical recovery, so it should not be used to plan return to play. The small heat index association is not clinically meaningful according to the authors, so it cannot set return-to-play timing. The study does not test return-to-play criteria and cannot be used to clear an athlete for return to play.

records.sourceFile: Therapeutic potential for cannabinoids in sports medicine - Current literature review.pdf

paper.citation: Naik H, Trojian TH. Therapeutic Potential for Cannabinoids in Sports Medicine: Current Literature Review. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2021;20(7):345-350.
paper.abstract: The review compares cannabidiol and delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol through the endocannabinoid system and summarizes their theoretical benefits and current U.S. legal status for common sports medicine conditions, to help clinicians answer questions from athletes and active patients.
paper.tldr: This is a clinician guide rather than trial evidence. Cannabidiol shows anti-inflammatory and analgesic effects mainly in animal and in vitro work, and human sports medicine trials are lacking. The authors do not recommend CBD for concussion and do not recommend medical marijuana containing THC.
paper.methods: Narrative literature review. The article does not describe a search strategy, inclusion criteria or quality appraisal.
paper.findings: Covers CB1, CB2, TRPV1, serotonin and GPR55 pharmacology. For osteoarthritis, cannabinoid receptors are found in cartilage and synovium, and the authors cite mostly preclinical work suggesting pain relief and possible disease modification, while noting CBD is not an FDA-approved treatment. For concussion, the authors state that trials do not exist and they do not recommend use. CBD had little effect on anxiety under low stress and mixed effects under stress; one study found 300 mg more anxiolytic than 150 or 600 mg, and another found 600 mg increased anxiety in a high-paranoia group. Cardiovascular findings are inconsistent, and the cited studies were done at rest rather than during exercise.
paper.limitations: The review is narrative and unsystematic, so the choice of evidence is not transparent. Most mechanistic and chronic pain support is preclinical, and human trials, dosing, safety and long-term effects remain unresolved in sports medicine. Adverse effects listed (drug interactions, liver enzyme elevation, diarrhea, fatigue, somnolence) come from epilepsy and psychiatric populations. Legal and market content is U.S.-specific and reflects 2020-2021 sources.
paper.practicalImplications: Expect athletes and active patients to ask about CBD for osteoarthritis, pain, concussion and pre-competition anxiety. Explain that the evidence is mostly animal or in vitro, that CBD is not recommended for concussion, and that the authors advise against medical marijuana containing THC because nonprescription THC products are not federally legal. The authors' only dosing comment is that 600 mg appears a poor choice for performance anxiety, which comes from non-athlete studies.
paper.athleteDev: The review contains no performance outcome data in athletes. Its cardiovascular and anxiety evidence is resting or non-sport based, and the authors state that CBD has not been studied for sports performance anxiety. It cannot support a performance or pre-competition dosing recommendation.
paper.rtp: This review cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It contains no trials of cannabinoids for concussion or injury recovery, and the authors do not recommend CBD for concussion at this time.

records.sourceFile: Vitamin D for improved bone health and prevention of stress fractures - A review of the literature.pdf

paper.citation: Lawley R, Syrop IP, Fredericson M. Vitamin D for Improved Bone Health and Prevention of Stress Fractures: A Review of the Literature. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2020;19(6):202-208.
paper.abstract: Reviews vitamin D physiology, status measurement and bone health, then the evidence linking vitamin D status and supplementation with stress fractures in adolescents, military recruits and athletes.
paper.tldr: Vitamin D status and stress fracture risk appear linked in athletes and recruits, but the studies are heterogeneous and mostly observational. The authors recommend vitamin D3 to maintain status in high-risk athletes, but the review does not set a dose or target level for them.
paper.methods: Narrative literature review. The article does not describe a search strategy, inclusion criteria or quality appraisal.
paper.findings: Indoor athletes are at greater risk of low 25(OH)D, though insufficiency is also reported in outdoor athletes and one study of female distance runners found mostly adequate status. A meta-analysis of eight military studies (2,634 personnel) found lower 25(OH)D in stress fracture cases, and cohorts of Finnish and Royal Marine recruits linked lower baseline 25(OH)D to stress fracture. In 37 British Army recruits, recovery from lower-limb stress fracture took about 10 weeks with sufficient 25(OH)D, 12 with insufficient and 13 with deficient levels. In female Navy recruits, 2000 mg calcium plus 800 IU vitamin D for 8 weeks gave a 20% lower stress fracture incidence, and in young female runners vitamin D intake gave an adjusted hazard ratio of 0.67 (0.34 to 1.31).
paper.limitations: No search method or quality appraisal is described. Athlete evidence is mostly observational and small, and the authors describe a non-significant hazard ratio (CI 0.34 to 1.31) as protective. Bone density trials in children and older adults are mixed, and a meta-analysis of 81 RCTs found no fracture or meaningful BMD benefit in older adults. Vitamin D thresholds differ by organization, and the authors note that 25(OH)D may not be the best marker.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors recommend vitamin D3 to maintain 25(OH)D status in athletes at high stress-fracture risk and cite thresholds of supplementing below 30 ng/mL (Shuler) or keeping 32 to 50 ng/mL (Female Athlete Triad Coalition), with 800 to 2000 IU daily suggested for high-risk individuals in a cited concept review. They state the athlete data are not strong enough to support a specific dose or target. Vitamin D is described as safe above usual intakes, though one trial reported more kidney stones in women.
paper.athleteDev: The review does not support a dose or target serum level for athletic performance. It cites Cannell's suggestion that 50 ng/mL may be ideal for performance, but the authors say the athlete data are not strong enough to set a dose or target for bone health.
paper.rtp: The only recovery data are military: 37 recruits with sufficient 25(OH)D recovered from lower-limb stress fractures faster than those insufficient or deficient. This does not give a return-to-sport protocol, and the review cannot set return-to-play criteria or a dosing plan for an injured athlete.
